apmo-2004-01.title: Extremal elements
apmo-2004-01.body:
**$2\in S$:** for any $k\in S$, $\frac{k+k}{(k,k)}=2\in S$.

**No odd elements.** Suppose $S$ contains odd numbers and let $k$ be the largest one ($S$ is finite). Since $(k,2)=1$, $\frac{k+2}{1}=k+2\in S$; it is odd and larger than $k$ — contradiction.

**No element other than $2$.** Suppose not, and let $\ell$ be the smallest element of $S$ with $\ell>2$. It is even, so $(\ell,2)=2$ and $\frac{\ell+2}{2}=\frac\ell2+1\in S$. Since $\ell\ge4$, we have $2<\frac\ell2+1<\ell$, contradicting the choice of $\ell$.

So $S=\{2\}$, and indeed $\frac{2+2}{2}=2\in S$.

**Answer:** $S=\{2\}$.

apmo-2004-02.title: Euler line and the centroid
apmo-2004-02.body:
If $O=H$ (equilateral triangle) all three areas are $0$ and there is nothing to prove. Otherwise let $\ell$ be the line $OH$ (the Euler line); it contains the centroid $G$. Write $d(X)$ for the distance from $X$ to $\ell$, so $[XOH]=\frac12\,OH\cdot d(X)$.

Of the three vertices, two lie in the same closed half-plane of $\ell$; say $B$ and $C$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Then $d(M)=\frac{d(B)+d(C)}2$ (the distance to a line is an affine function on a half-plane).

$G$ lies on segment $AM$ with $AG=2\,GM$, and $G\in\ell$. Dropping perpendiculars from $A$ and $M$ to $\ell$ gives two similar right triangles with ratio $AG:GM=2$, hence $d(A)=2d(M)$ (if $A\in\ell$ then also $M\in\ell$ and both distances are $0$). Therefore
$$[BOH]+[COH]=\frac{OH}{2}\bigl(d(B)+d(C)\bigr)=\frac{OH}2\cdot2d(M)=\frac{OH}2\,d(A)=[AOH]. \qquad ∎$$

apmo-2004-02.title: Vectors from the circumcentre
apmo-2004-02.body:
Put the origin at $O$ and let $\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf c$ be the position vectors of the vertices. It is well known (and easy to check: $(\mathbf b+\mathbf c)\cdot(\mathbf b-\mathbf c)=|\mathbf b|^2-|\mathbf c|^2=0$, so $\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c$ lies on the altitude from $A$, and similarly on the others) that $\mathbf h=\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c$.

The signed area of $XOH$ is $\frac12\,\mathbf x\times\mathbf h$ (2D cross product). Then
$$\mathbf a\times\mathbf h+\mathbf b\times\mathbf h+\mathbf c\times\mathbf h=(\mathbf a+\mathbf b+\mathbf c)\times\mathbf h=\mathbf h\times\mathbf h=0 .$$
So the three signed areas $s_A,s_B,s_C$ add up to $0$. Two of them have the same sign (or are $0$), say $s_B,s_C\ge0$ or both $\le0$; then $s_A=-(s_B+s_C)$ gives $|s_A|=|s_B|+|s_C|$, i.e. $[AOH]=[BOH]+[COH]$. ∎

apmo-2004-03.title: A parity identity for triples
apmo-2004-03.body:
Let $n(p,q)$ be the number of lines of $\mathcal L$ separating $p$ and $q$.

**Key lemma.** For any three distinct points $p,q,r\in S$,
$$n(p,q)+n(q,r)+n(r,p)\equiv1\pmod2 .$$
Count, for each line $\ell\in\mathcal L$, how many of the pairs $\{p,q\},\{q,r\},\{r,p\}$ it separates.
- If $\ell$ passes through none of $p,q,r$, it splits them $3{+}0$ or $2{+}1$, separating $0$ or $2$ pairs — an even contribution.
- If $\ell$ passes through two of them (e.g. $\ell=pq$), it separates none of the pairs, since every pair has a point on $\ell$.
- Otherwise $\ell=ps$ (or $qs$, $rs$) with $s\in S\setminus\{p,q,r\}$, and it can only separate the opposite pair $\{q,r\}$.

So the sum is congruent mod $2$ to the number of pairs $(s,v)$, $s\in S\setminus\{p,q,r\}$, $v\in\{p,q,r\}$, such that line $sv$ separates the other two vertices. Fix $s$ (not on any of the lines $pq,qr,rp$, as no three points are collinear):
- If $s$ is inside triangle $pqr$, the rays $sp,sq,sr$ divide the full angle into three angles each $<180^\circ$, so each of the three lines $sp,sq,sr$ separates the other two vertices: $3$ pairs.
- If $s$ is outside, the triangle lies in an open half-plane bounded by a line through $s$, so the rays $sp,sq,sr$ lie in an open half-plane. The line along the middle ray separates the other two points, and the lines along the outer rays do not: exactly $1$ pair.

Each $s$ contributes an odd number, so the sum is $\equiv|S|-3=2001\equiv1\pmod2$.

**Colouring.** Fix $p\in S$ and colour it blue; colour $q\ne p$ blue if $n(p,q)$ is odd and red if it is even. Pairs containing $p$ behave correctly by definition. For $q,r\ne p$, the lemma gives $n(q,r)\equiv1+n(p,q)+n(p,r)$, so $n(q,r)$ is odd $\iff$ $n(p,q)\equiv n(p,r)\pmod 2$ $\iff$ $q,r$ have the same colour. ∎

apmo-2004-04.title: Composite cases and Wilson's theorem
apmo-2004-04.body:
Let $N=(n-1)!$. For $n\le5$, $N<n(n+1)$ ($1<2,\ 1<6,\ 2<12,\ 6<20,\ 24<30$), so the floor is $0$. Let $n\ge6$.

**Lemma 1.** If $u\le n+1$ is an odd composite number, then $u\mid N$. Write $u=st$ with $3\le s\le t$. If $s<t$, then $s<t\le\frac u3\le\frac{n+1}3<n-1$, so $s,t$ are distinct factors of $N$. If $s=t$, then $s$ and $2s$ are distinct and $2s\le s^2-2\le n-1$ (as $s\ge3$), so $s\cdot2s$ divides $N$.

**Lemma 2.** If $e\le n+1$ is even and $e\ge6$, then $2e\mid N$. Write $e=2f$, $f\ge3$. If $f\ne4$, the numbers $4$ and $f\le\frac{n+1}2\le n-1$ are distinct factors of $N$ with product $2e$. If $f=4$ then $n\ge7$, and $2\cdot4\cdot6=48$ is divisible by $2e=16$.

Since $n\ge6$, $n$ and $n+1$ are not both prime. Exactly one of them is even; call it $e$ (so $e\ge6$) and the other one $u$.

**Case 1: $n$ and $n+1$ both composite.** By the lemmas $u\mid N$ and $2e\mid N$; as $\gcd(u,2e)=1$, $2n(n+1)\mid N$, so $\frac{N}{n(n+1)}$ is an even integer.

**Case 2: $n$ is prime** ($n\ge7$, $e=n+1$). By Lemma 2, $N=2(n+1)K$ for an integer $K$. By Wilson's theorem $N\equiv-1\pmod n$, so $n\mid N+n+1$; also $(n+1)\mid N+n+1$, and $\gcd(n,n+1)=1$, so $N+n+1=n(n+1)L$ for an integer $L$. Now $\frac{N+n+1}{n+1}=2K+1=nL$ is odd, so $L$ is odd. Finally
$$\frac{N}{n(n+1)}=L-\frac1n,\qquad\text{so}\qquad\left\lfloor\frac{N}{n(n+1)}\right\rfloor=L-1,$$
which is even.

**Case 3: $n+1$ is prime** ($n+1\ge7$, $e=n$). By Lemma 2, $N=2nK$. By Wilson, $n!\equiv-1\pmod{n+1}$; since $n\equiv-1$, this gives $N\equiv1$, so $(n+1)\mid N+n$; also $n\mid N+n$, hence $N+n=n(n+1)L$. Then $\frac{N+n}{n}=2K+1=(n+1)L$ is odd, so $L$ is odd, and
$$\left\lfloor\frac{N}{n(n+1)}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor L-\frac1{n+1}\right\rfloor=L-1$$
is even. ∎

apmo-2004-05.title: Two discriminants
apmo-2004-05.body:
We prove the stronger inequality
$$(a^2+2)(b^2+2)(c^2+2)\ge3(a+b+c)^2,\tag{$*$}$$
which suffices because $(a+b+c)^2-3(ab+bc+ca)=\frac12\left[(a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-a)^2\right]\ge0$.

Let $P=(b^2+2)(c^2+2)$. Then $(*)$ is
$$(P-3)a^2-6(b+c)a+2P-3(b+c)^2\ge0 .$$
Its leading coefficient $P-3=b^2c^2+2b^2+2c^2+1$ is positive, so it is enough that the discriminant is $\le0$:
$$9(b+c)^2\le(P-3)\bigl(2P-3(b+c)^2\bigr)\iff 0\le 2P^2-3P(b+c)^2-6P\iff 2P-3(b+c)^2-6\ge0 .$$
Expanding, $2P-3(b+c)^2-6=(2c^2+1)b^2-6cb+(c^2+2)$, a quadratic in $b$ with positive leading coefficient and discriminant
$$36c^2-4(2c^2+1)(c^2+2)=-8\left(c^4-2c^2+1\right)=-8(c^2-1)^2\le0 .$$
So it is $\ge0$, which proves $(*)$ and the inequality. Equality holds for $a=b=c=1$. ∎

apmo-2004-05.title: Pigeonhole on signs, then Cauchy–Schwarz
apmo-2004-05.body:
Among $a^2-1$, $b^2-1$, $c^2-1$ two have the same sign (counting $0$ as either); by symmetry say $(a^2-1)(b^2-1)\ge0$. Then
$$(a^2+2)(b^2+2)=a^2b^2+2a^2+2b^2+4=3(a^2+b^2+1)+(a^2-1)(b^2-1)\ge3(a^2+b^2+1).$$
By Cauchy–Schwarz,
$$(a^2+b^2+1)(1+1+c^2)\ge(a\cdot1+b\cdot1+1\cdot c)^2=(a+b+c)^2 .$$
Hence
$$(a^2+2)(b^2+2)(c^2+2)\ge3(a+b+c)^2\ge9(ab+bc+ca). \qquad ∎$$
